title: ONAN WANTED TAMAR’S BODY—BUT REFUSED THE RESPONSIBILITY THAT CAME WITH HER
paragraphs:
ONAN WANTED TAMAR’S BODY—BUT REFUSED THE RESPONSIBILITY THAT CAME WITH HER
He kept going into his brother’s widow while secretly making sure she could never receive what he had been commanded to give her. Genesis 38 is not merely an ancient sexual scandal. It is a terrifying portrait of what happens when someone wants the privilege of intimacy while rejecting the responsibility of covenant—and hidden inside this disturbing family story is a road that eventually leads all the way to Jesus Christ.
There is a sentence in Genesis that becomes more disturbing the longer you sit with it.
Not because Scripture is trying to be graphic.
Not because God delights in exposing sexual scandal.
But because one man found a way to appear obedient while privately arranging things so that obedience would never cost him what he wanted to keep.
His name was Onan.
And Tamar was the woman caught in the consequences.
Read the Hebrew carefully:
"וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוּדָה לְאוֹנָן בֹּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ"
Vayyomer Yehudah le-Onan, bo el-eshet achikha, veyabbem otah, vehaqem zera le-achikha.
Judah tells Onan, in essence:
“Go in to your brother’s wife, perform the duty of a brother-in-law toward her, and raise up offspring for your brother.”
Genesis 38:8.
The Hebrew expression וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ — vehaqem zera le-achikha means to “raise up offspring for your brother.”
That is crucial.
Er, Tamar’s husband, had died without a child. Judah therefore commanded his surviving son Onan to fulfill the family obligation toward Tamar and his deceased brother.

Later Mosaic legislation would formally describe the related institution in Deuteronomy 25:5–10: when a brother died without a son under the circumstances described there, his surviving brother was to take responsibility for the widow, and the firstborn son would preserve the dead brother’s name in Israel.
Genesis 38 predates the giving of that Mosaic legislation, so we should not carelessly pretend that every later legal detail had already been formally enacted in exactly the same form.
But the underlying purpose in Genesis 38 is unmistakable because the narrator tells us directly.
Onan understood exactly what was expected of him.
And he did not want it.
Here is where the story becomes painfully uncomfortable.
Onan did not simply refuse Tamar.
Had the story merely said, “Onan would not take her,” we would be reading a different story.
Instead:
"וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע"
Vayyeda Onan ki lo lo yihyeh hazzara.
“Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
Genesis 38:9.
There is his motive.
Scripture opens the locked room of his heart.
He knew.
The issue was not ignorance.
It was not confusion.
It was not an accident.
He knew the child would not be counted as his.
And because the benefit would belong to his dead brother’s line rather than ultimately serving his own interests, Onan deliberately prevented Tamar from conceiving.
The Hebrew continues:
"וְהָיָה אִם־בָּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו"
Whenever he went in to his brother’s wife, he deliberately wasted his seed on the ground “so as not to give offspring to his brother.”
Do not rush past those words.
Whenever.
The Hebrew construction describes repeated behavior.
This was not one moment of weakness.
Not one frightened decision.
Not one impulsive failure followed by remorse.
Onan continued taking Tamar sexually while deliberately ensuring that the very purpose for which he had been given responsibility toward her would never be fulfilled.
He wanted access without obligation.
Intimacy without sacrifice.
The woman without the responsibility.
The privilege without the covenantal cost.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that, from the outside, he could appear to be fulfilling his duty.
He went to Tamar.
But God saw what happened when nobody else was watching.
That is where this ancient story suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Because Onan’s temptation did not die with Onan.
We have simply learned how to dress it differently.
How many people want the comfort of another person without carrying responsibility for that person?
How many want sex without covenant?
Marriage without sacrifice?
Family without faithfulness?
Church without surrender?
Grace without repentance?
Jesus as Savior while quietly resisting Jesus as Lord?
How many of us have discovered sophisticated ways of looking obedient publicly while arranging our private lives so obedience never interferes with what we really want?
That is the nerve Genesis 38 touches.
And before we use Onan’s story as a weapon against somebody else, we should allow Scripture to turn the light toward us.
Because you do not have to be Onan to possess an Onan-shaped corner of the heart.
A place where you say yes with your mouth while your choices quietly say no.
A place where you want what God gives but resist what God asks.
A place where you want the pleasure, comfort, reputation, relationship, ministry, blessing, forgiveness, platform, marriage, influence, or security—but not the surrender attached to it.
People can be fooled by religious appearances.
God cannot.
Genesis says:
"וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה"
Vayyera be'enei YHWH asher asah.
“What he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”
Genesis 38:10.
Notice the language.
What he did was evil before God.

The passage does not permit us to reduce Onan’s sin to a slogan about one isolated sexual act. The narrator has already supplied the motive: Onan knew the offspring would not belong to him, and he intentionally acted “so as not to give offspring to his brother.”
His sexual behavior was inseparable from his selfish refusal of responsibility.
He was exploiting the arrangement while sabotaging its purpose.
And Tamar paid the price.
That matters because Tamar can disappear when this passage is discussed only as a debate about male sexuality.
But Genesis does not allow her to disappear.
She had already buried a husband.
Now the man charged with helping preserve her deceased husband’s family line repeatedly came to her while secretly making sure she remained childless.
Then Onan died.
And Tamar was left waiting again.
Judah promised that when his younger son Shelah grew up, Tamar would be given to him.
But Judah became afraid.
So Tamar waited.
And waited.
Shelah grew.
The promise did not.
Imagine what that waiting meant in her world.

She could not simply reinvent her life according to twenty-first-century expectations. Her future, household security, motherhood, and place within the family structure were entangled with decisions being made by men around her.
Er failed.
Onan failed.
Then Judah failed to give her Shelah as promised.
Three times, Tamar's future was affected by men who possessed more social power than she did.
Then Genesis 38 becomes even more scandalous.
Tamar disguises herself.
Judah sees her, fails to recognize her, assumes she is a prostitute, and sleeps with her.
She conceives.
Months later, Judah hears that Tamar is pregnant.
His reaction is horrifyingly swift.
He calls for judgment.
But Tamar possesses Judah’s seal, cord, and staff—the identifying objects he had given as a pledge.
She sends them to him.
No screaming.
No public speech.
Just evidence.
“Recognize, please, whose these are.”
And suddenly Judah is standing face-to-face with himself.
Then comes one of the great confession moments in Genesis:
"צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי"
Tzadqah mimmeni.
“She is more righteous than I.”
Genesis 38:26.
And Judah explains why:
Because he had not given her to Shelah his son.
The man who was prepared to condemn Tamar was forced to recognize his own failure.
That sentence should frighten every religious person who finds it easier to identify somebody else’s scandal than his own sin.
Sometimes we are furious about the visible evidence of someone else's brokenness while remaining strangely merciful toward the hidden compromises that helped create it.
Judah looked at Tamar and saw disgrace.
God was forcing Judah to look at Judah.
And something changed.
Genesis 38 does not leave Judah as the same man.
Earlier, in Genesis 37, Judah was the brother who proposed selling Joseph.
Later, when Benjamin’s freedom and his father Jacob’s heart are at stake, Judah becomes the brother willing to offer himself in Benjamin’s place.
“Please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord.”
Genesis 44:33.
The man who once surrendered a brother to save himself becomes a man willing to surrender himself to save a brother.
That is transformation.
Not perfection.
Transformation.
And now the story becomes breathtaking.
Because Tamar became pregnant with twins.
Perez and Zerah.
Perez became part of the line that eventually produced David.
And centuries later, when Matthew opens his Gospel and records the genealogy of Jesus Christ, he does something ancient genealogies could easily have avoided.
He mentions Tamar.
“Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar…”
Matthew 1:3.
There she is.
The scandal was not erased.
The complicated history was not airbrushed.
Tamar's name stands in the genealogy that leads toward Christ.
Not because sin became righteous.
Not because deception became God's ideal.
Not because sexual brokenness ceased to matter.
But because human sin cannot outmaneuver the redemptive purposes of God.
Read that again if your past embarrasses you.
Human sin cannot outmaneuver the redemptive purposes of God.
The family line was messy.
God was faithful.
Judah had failed.
God was faithful.
Tamar had been wronged.
God was faithful.
Onan acted selfishly.
God was faithful.
Generations passed.
Kings rose and fell.
And eventually another Son of Judah appeared.
Jesus Christ.
But unlike Onan, Jesus did not take while refusing to give.
Jesus gave Himself.
Onan protected his own interests at another person's expense.
Christ surrendered His own life for sinners.
Onan refused a costly responsibility because the resulting legacy would not be his.
Jesus willingly embraced the cross to bring people who had nothing to offer Him into the family of God.
Onan's story is curved inward toward self.
The Gospel opens outward in sacrificial love.
Jesus said:
“The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
Mark 10:45.
There is the greater Man.
There is the faithful Bridegroom.
There is the One who does not use His bride.
He dies for her.
Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Ephesians 5:25.
That is why Genesis 38 must eventually lead us beyond outrage at Onan.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of bad people over there being exposed.
It is the story of sinners being brought into the light and offered mercy through the blood of Jesus Christ.
Maybe your hidden sin is sexual.
Maybe it is not.
Maybe nobody knows what you keep deleting.
Maybe nobody knows what happens when the door closes.
Maybe people at church know one version of you while your phone knows another.
Maybe you keep taking emotionally from someone you have no intention of loving faithfully.
Maybe you want someone’s body but not their heart.
Maybe you keep another person close enough to satisfy your loneliness while knowing you will never give them honest commitment.
Maybe your hidden compromise has nothing to do with sexuality at all.
Maybe you want God's provision but not God's commands.
His forgiveness but not repentance.
His heaven but not His holiness.
His promises but not His authority.
And perhaps you have become very good at making partial obedience look complete.
Onan reminds us that God sees the difference.
But if conviction is rising inside you right now, do not mistake conviction for an invitation to despair.
The Bible did not preserve Genesis 38 merely to tell us that God sees hidden evil.
It preserved a story in which disgrace, failure, selfishness, injustice, confession, and a deeply broken family history somehow become part of the road toward Bethlehem.
That is grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Grace that enters where evil has done its damage and begins rewriting what sin tried to destroy.
Maybe that is why you needed this story today.
You thought your chapter disqualified the whole book.
Jesus is still writing.
You thought the things done to you had permanently named you.
Jesus is still writing.
You thought the things you did in secret meant God could never use what remained.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin.
Turn away from it.
And come to Christ.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23.
But Scripture does not stop there.
We are “justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 3:24.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending.
Not hiding.
Not performing.
Not finding somebody whose scandal looks worse than yours so you can temporarily feel clean.
Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Grace offered freely.
Repentance demanded honestly.
Forgiveness purchased completely.
A new life made possible through Him.
Where are you taking while refusing to give?
Where are you enjoying privilege while avoiding responsibility?
Where have you learned to imitate obedience while secretly protecting rebellion?
And what would happen if tonight you stopped hiding it from Jesus?
He already knows.
The question is whether you will bring it into the light.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can make one honest declaration.
And believers—do not turn that comment section into a courtroom.
Make it somewhere wounded people encounter truth and grace.
Pray for one another.
Point one another toward Christ.
Supporting Gospel-centered teaching can itself be one practical way to help truthful Christian content reach more people. Scripture calls us to glorify God with our whole lives.
Jesus Christ.
The One who walked willingly into humanity's scandal.
The One who carried sin He never committed.
The One who was stripped, mocked, crucified, and buried.
The One who rose.
The One who still receives repentant sinners.
Tamar's story survived.
Judah's failure was exposed.
Onan's secret was seen.
And through a family history no public-relations department would ever have chosen, the genealogy kept moving until Matthew could write:
That is the Gospel's strange beauty.
God does not need a spotless family history to accomplish a holy purpose.
He creates redeemed people through a spotless Savior.
So when Satan points at the chapter you wish had never been written, point him toward the cross.
Because the chapter that looks like the end of your story may become the very place where grace teaches you that Jesus still holds the pen.
